payload.title: What Are the Mexican Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
protect_keywords: 10 of the most fascinating wedding traditions in mexico (old URL; SEO to quantify US and AU)
payload.audience: Couples in their 30s interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, AUD 150k+ budget
payload.reader: An Australian couple in their 30s with a generous budget, often with a Mexican partner or parents, who want to understand what the families will expect (padrinos and madrinas, lazo, arras, Mass and civil ceremony, music, dances, tornaboda), honour the customs respectfully, and decide whether to marry in Mexico (Smartraveller: exercise a high degree of caution overall, higher levels in some states) or bring the customs into a wedding at home.
payload.goal: Read the free Wedded Wonderland digital magazine (primary CTA); secondary, in-context invitation to speak with a Wedded Advisor placed after the 'for Australians' section.
payload.angle: Most lists turn a Mexican wedding into a party and a bill. We walk through it in wedding order as families live it: the padrinos and madrinas who stand with the couple, the lazo and arras inside the Catholic Mass, the civil ceremony that makes it legal, then the callejoneada, mariachi, dances and the tornaboda. Meanings are stated only where Mexico's culture ministry, INAH, UNESCO, Britannica or the RAE state them; everything else is written as living practice that varies by region and family. We close with what Australians need, as Smartraveller and the Australian Embassy in Mexico City word it, and which regions couples choose outside Smartraveller's higher-level areas.
must_include: One early framing line: customs vary by region and family and some Indigenous communities keep their own; tie a custom to a region only where a source does

About 12 numbered sections in wedding order: padrinos and madrinas, lazo, arras, Catholic Mass, civil ceremony, callejoneada, mariachi, money dance, la víbora de la mar, cookies and cake, tornaboda, UNESCO, for Australians
Spanish terms with accents exactly as sources give them (víbora, bendición); inline definitions
Arras and money dance described with no amounts or counts beyond the 13 coins as sourced
UNESCO 'Mariachi, string music, song and trumpet' (2011) quoted only as far as its own text links to weddings, if confirmed live

Section for Australians: Smartraveller overall level and the higher-level states, update date (as at November 2026), hurricane season, same-sex recognition once, entry line, Australian Embassy Mexico City for CNI and notarial, 'Getting married overseas', 'check with the registry and the embassy, including any fees'; regions only outside higher-level areas; Mexican-Australian weddings at home
FAQ of 5 to 7 questions with no amounts, keeping the old page's FAQ query coverage
Internal links: /destinations/latin-america-caribbean/mexico and /10-tips-for-planning-a-destination-wedding-in-mexico (link, do not compete); Filipino and Brazilian traditions drafts where natural

tradition_plan.note: Planner (wedding-planner-sme) runs batch A and batch B in parallel, scratch folders 02-research/batch-a and 02-research/batch-b, 15 min HARD by the clock, save after every 3 facts, no extra sourcing rounds, never retry a declined call. Preferred sources: gob.mx/cultura, Secretaría de Turismo / visitmexico.com, INAH, museums, ich.unesco.org, Britannica, RAE, academic sources. Never competitor wedding sites, vendor blogs or Wikipedia. Unsourced customs are written as living practice with no meaning or origin as fact and no [[VERIFY]] marker; 'often told' at most once per post. Source gaps go in the run report only (authority rule).
